::: {.lead}
A coordinate tells a program *where* an object is. Almost everything else a
game needs to know — where the object is going, how fast, in which direction
it was hit, where the enemy is relative to the player — is a *change* of
position. The mathematical object that describes such a change is the vector.
This chapter defines vectors geometrically and algebraically, separates them
carefully from points, and uses them to move objects frame by frame.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary scalar vector magnitude direction component displacement velocity zero-vector opposite-vector free-vector >}}

## 2.1 Scalars and vectors

Some quantities in a game are described completely by one number: the
player's health (75), the time left (42 s), the mass of a crate (20 kg), the
speed shown on a car's dashboard (90 km/h). Such quantities are called
**scalars**. Other quantities cannot be described by one number, because they
also have a direction. "The wind blows at 5 m/s" is incomplete; "the wind
blows at 5 m/s towards the east" is a full description. Quantities that have
both a size and a direction are called **vectors**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Scalar and vector"}
A **scalar** is a quantity that has only a size (a single real number). A
**vector** is a quantity that has a size, called its **magnitude**, and a
**direction**.
:::

![A scalar is one number; a vector also has a direction.](images/scalar-vector.png){#fig-scalar width=86%}

Pairs of related quantities illustrate the difference. **Distance** (how far)
is a scalar; **displacement** (how far *and* which way) is a vector. **Speed**
(how fast) is a scalar; **velocity** (how fast *and* which way) is a vector.
Gravity in a game is a vector — usually of magnitude 9.8 m/s² pointing down —
and so is the force of an explosion that throws a character away from its
centre.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — Classifying game quantities"}
Decide whether each value in a platformer is a scalar or a vector.

1. The score, 12 400: one number — **scalar**.
2. "The player moves 3 units to the right per frame": size 3 and a
   direction — **vector** (a velocity).
3. The magnitude of that movement, 3 units per frame: **scalar** (a speed).
4. The knockback "4 units away from the enemy": **vector**.
5. The cooldown of a skill, 2.5 s: **scalar**.
:::

## 2.2 The geometric view: arrows

Geometrically, a vector is drawn as an **arrow** — a directed line segment.
The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the arrow points in the
direction of the vector. The starting point of the arrow is its **tail** and
the pointed end is its **head** (@fig-arrow).

![A vector drawn as an arrow, and three arrows that represent the same vector.](images/vector-arrow.png){#fig-arrow width=88%}

A vector has a magnitude and a direction, but **no position**. The arrow may be
drawn anywhere: two arrows with the same length and the same direction
represent the same vector, even if one is drawn at the origin and the other in
the corner of the level. In @fig-arrow all three arrows on the right are the
same vector, "3 to the right and 2 up". This is exactly how movement works in
a game: "move 3 right and 2 up" means the same thing for the player standing
at the start and for the player standing at the exit.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.2 — Equal vectors"}
Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same magnitude and the same
direction, regardless of where their arrows are drawn.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Treating two arrows as different vectors because they start at different
points. Position belongs to *points*, not to vectors. Two enemies that both
move "2 units left per frame" have equal velocity vectors, although they are
in different places.
:::

## 2.3 Components and notation

A program cannot store an arrow; it stores numbers. If the tail of an arrow is
placed at the origin, the head lands on a point whose coordinates describe the
vector completely. These numbers are the **components** of the vector: the
signed number of units the vector moves along each axis.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.3 — Components"}
A 2D vector $\mathbf{v}$ with components $v_x$ and $v_y$ is written
$\mathbf{v} = (v_x, v_y)$; a 3D vector is written $\mathbf{v} = (v_x, v_y, v_z)$.
The component $v_x$ is the change along the $x$-axis and $v_y$ the change along
the $y$-axis. If an arrow goes from the tail $(x_1, y_1)$ to the head
$(x_2, y_2)$, its components are $(x_2 - x_1,\ y_2 - y_1)$: **head minus tail**.
:::

Vectors are printed in **bold** ($\mathbf{v}$) or written by hand with an
arrow above the letter ($\vec{v}$). In mathematics books they are often written
as columns,
$$
\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix},
$$
which is the same vector as $(3, -2)$; the column form becomes important when
vectors are multiplied by matrices in week 5.

![Reading the components of an arrow: head minus tail.](images/components.png){#fig-components width=70%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — Components from a drawing"}
In @fig-components an arrow starts at $(1, 4)$ and ends at $(5, 1)$.

1. $v_x = 5 - 1 = 4$: four units to the right.
2. $v_y = 1 - 4 = -3$: three units *down* — a negative component means the
   negative direction of the axis.
3. $\mathbf{v} = (4, -3)$. The same vector, drawn from the origin, would end at
   the point $(4, -3)$.
:::

The sign of each component tells the direction along its axis; a zero
component means no movement along that axis. The vector $(0, 5)$ points
straight up, $(-2, 0)$ straight left.

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
Game code stores vectors in small types such as `Vector2` (two `float`
components) and `Vector3` (three). The components are read with `.x`, `.y`
and `.z`.

```csharp
Vector2 jump = new Vector2(4f, -3f);   // 4 right, 3 down
float right = jump.x;                   // 4
float down  = jump.y;                   // -3
```
:::

### The algebraic view: a vector is an ordered list of numbers

Once a vector is written as components, nothing forces the list to have two or
three entries, or the entries to be distances. Algebraically, a vector is
simply an **ordered list of numbers**; the number of entries is its
**dimension**. Games use such lists constantly. A colour on screen is a
3-vector $(r, g, b)$ of red, green and blue intensities — or a 4-vector
$(r, g, b, a)$ with an opacity $a$. The stats of a character, $(\text{strength},
\text{agility}, \text{intelligence})$, form a 3-vector. The input of a touch
joystick is a 2-vector read once per frame.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.4 — Vector of dimension n"}
An $n$-dimensional vector is an ordered list of $n$ real numbers
$(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n)$. Two vectors are equal exactly when they have the same
dimension and all corresponding components are equal.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — The input of a virtual joystick"}
A mobile game shows a virtual joystick. Every frame it reports a 2D vector
whose components lie between $-1$ and $1$: $x$ for left–right and $y$ for
down–up.

1. The player pushes the stick fully to the right: the input is $(1, 0)$.
2. Pushed halfway up and to the left: about $(-0.5, 0.5)$.
3. Released: $(0, 0)$, the zero vector — the character stands still.
4. The *direction* of the input decides where the character walks; its
   *magnitude* (how far the stick is pushed) decides whether it walks or runs.
:::

### Basis vectors

Each axis has a vector of length 1 that points along its positive direction.
These **standard basis vectors** are written
$$
\mathbf{i} = (1, 0, 0), \qquad \mathbf{j} = (0, 1, 0), \qquad \mathbf{k} = (0, 0, 1)
$$
(in 2D, $\mathbf{i} = (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{j} = (0, 1)$). Every vector is a sum of
copies of them: the components say how many copies of each are needed. For
example, $(4, -3) = 4\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}$: four steps along $\mathbf{i}$ and
three steps against $\mathbf{j}$ (@fig-basis). Game engines give the basis vectors names
such as `Vector3.right`, `Vector3.up` and `Vector3.forward`; in a $y$-up
left-handed engine these are $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{k}$.

![The vector $(4, -3)$ built from four copies of $\mathbf{i}$ and three copies of $-\mathbf{j}$.](images/basis-vectors.png){#fig-basis width=56%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.5 — Standard basis"}
The standard basis vectors $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$ have length 1 and
point along $+x$, $+y$ and $+z$. A vector with components $(v_x, v_y, v_z)$ equals
$v_x\mathbf{i} + v_y\mathbf{j} + v_z\mathbf{k}$.
:::

## 2.4 Points and displacement vectors

In everyday speech, "position" and "direction" are easily confused, and the
same notation $(4, -3)$ is used for both. They are, however, different kinds of
object. A **point** is a location: it answers *where?* A **vector** is a
change: it answers *how far and which way?* A point can be thought of as the
vector that leads from the origin to it, but a vector by itself is not
anchored anywhere.

The most common way to obtain a vector in a game is to compare two points.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.6 — Displacement vector"}
The **displacement vector** from point $A$ to point $B$ is
$$
\mathbf{d} = B - A = (B_x - A_x,\ B_y - A_y).
$$
It is the movement that takes an object from $A$ to $B$.
:::

The order of the subtraction carries the meaning: $B - A$ points **from $A$
to $B$** ("end minus start"). Reversing the order gives the opposite
movement.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.7 — Negative vector and zero vector"}
The **negative** of $\mathbf{v} = (v_x, v_y)$ is $-\mathbf{v} = (-v_x, -v_y)$: it
has the same magnitude and the opposite direction. In particular
$A - B = -(B - A)$. The **zero vector** $\mathbf{0} = (0, 0)$ has magnitude 0
and no direction; it is the displacement from a point to itself.
:::

![The displacement from the enemy E to the player P, and its negative.](images/displacement.png){#fig-displacement width=76%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.4 — Enemy and player"}
An enemy stands at $E = (2, 7)$ and the player at $P = (6, 4)$
(@fig-displacement).

1. Displacement from the enemy to the player: $P - E = (6 - 2,\ 4 - 7) = (4, -3)$.
   The enemy must go 4 right and 3 down to reach the player.
2. Displacement from the player to the enemy: $E - P = (-4, 3)$, the negative
   of the first vector.
3. When the enemy hits the player, a **knockback** pushes the player *away*
   from the enemy, in the direction of $P - E = (4, -3)$; a pull towards the
   enemy uses $E - P$.
:::

Game engines do not enforce this distinction. In C# the same type,
`Vector3`, holds the position of an object (a point) and its velocity (a
vector), and the compiler will happily add two positions. Keeping the meaning
straight is the programmer's job, and good code makes it visible in its names:
`position`, `spawnPoint` and `target` for points; `velocity`, `offset`,
`direction` and `toPlayer` for vectors. A line such as
`Vector3 toPlayer = player - enemy;` documents itself: it is a displacement,
and its order — end minus start — can be checked at a glance.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Subtracting in the wrong order. "From $A$ to $B$" is always $B - A$. An enemy
that computes $E - P$ instead of $P - E$ walks *away* from the player.
:::

## 2.5 Moving a point with a vector

Adding a vector to a point moves the point: if $P$ is a point and $\mathbf{d}$
a displacement, then $P' = P + \mathbf{d}$ is the point reached from $P$ by
that displacement. The three operations between points and vectors are
summarised below; together they explain why the distinction of §2.4 matters.

| Operation | Result | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| point $-$ point | vector | the displacement between two locations |
| point $+$ vector | point | a location moved by a displacement |
| vector $+$ vector | vector | two displacements one after the other (week 2) |
| point $+$ point | — | meaningless: locations cannot be added |

: Operations with points and vectors. {#tbl-ops}

### Motion frame by frame

A moving object has a **velocity**: the displacement it makes in one unit of
time. Games often measure this unit in frames. If an object at $\mathbf{p}_0$
has a constant velocity $\mathbf{v}$ per frame, the game loop updates its
position once per frame:
$$
\mathbf{p}_{1} = \mathbf{p}_0 + \mathbf{v}, \quad
\mathbf{p}_{2} = \mathbf{p}_1 + \mathbf{v}, \quad \ldots \quad
\mathbf{p}_{k+1} = \mathbf{p}_k + \mathbf{v}.
$$
Adding the same vector $n$ times moves the object by $n$ times each component:
$$
\mathbf{p}_n = (p_{0x} + n\,v_x,\ \ p_{0y} + n\,v_y).
$$

![Five frames of constant velocity $\mathbf{v} = (2, 1)$ starting at $(1, 1)$.](images/per-frame.png){#fig-per-frame width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.5 — Where is the ship after 4 frames?"}
A ship starts at $\mathbf{p}_0 = (1, 1)$ with velocity $\mathbf{v} = (2, 1)$ per
frame (@fig-per-frame).

1. Frame 1: $(1 + 2,\ 1 + 1) = (3, 2)$.
2. Frame 2: $(5, 3)$; frame 3: $(7, 4)$.
3. Directly: $\mathbf{p}_4 = (1 + 4 \times 2,\ 1 + 4 \times 1) = (9, 5)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.6 — Choosing a velocity (the reverse question)"}
A homing missile at $(10, 7)$ must reach a target at $(4, 1)$ in exactly 3
frames with a constant velocity. Which velocity is needed?

1. Total displacement: $(4, 1) - (10, 7) = (-6, -6)$.
2. Three equal steps make up the total, so each step is a third of each
   component: $\mathbf{v} = (-2, -2)$.
3. Check: $(10, 7) + 3 \times (-2, -2) = (10 - 6,\ 7 - 6) = (4, 1)$. ✓
:::

The frame-based velocity is simple but has a flaw that week 2 repairs: if the
frame rate drops from 60 to 30 fps, an object moving "2 units per frame"
travels half as far per second. Real game code therefore stores velocity per
*second* and multiplies it by the frame time.

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
The update that runs once per frame:

```csharp
Vector2 position = new Vector2(1f, 1f);
Vector2 velocity = new Vector2(2f, 1f);   // units per frame
position = position + velocity;           // a point moved by a vector
```
:::

The mini-game below turns this rule into a puzzle: choose the velocity per
frame that lands a ship exactly on its target after a given number of frames.

{{< sim file="sims/vector-dash.html" poster="sims/vector-dash.png" title="Vector Dash: one velocity, n frames" kind="game" height="620" >}}

## 2.6 Vectors in three dimensions

Everything in this chapter extends to three dimensions by adding a third
component. A 3D vector $(v_x, v_y, v_z)$ moves $v_x$ units along $x$, $v_y$
along $y$ and $v_z$ along $z$; the displacement between two 3D points is again
end minus start, component by component.

In a world with $y$ up, a vector splits naturally into two parts that games
treat differently: the **vertical** part $(0, v_y, 0)$, which changes the
height, and the **horizontal** part $(v_x, 0, v_z)$, which moves along the
ground. A character that walks on flat ground has $v_y = 0$; a jump or a fall
changes only $v_y$.

![A drone flies from $A$ to $B$: the displacement has a horizontal and a vertical part.](images/drone-3d.png){#fig-drone width=74%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.7 — A delivery drone"}
A drone takes off at $A = (2, 0, 1)$ and delivers a parcel at
$B = (6, 5, -3)$ (@fig-drone).

1. Displacement: $B - A = (6 - 2,\ 5 - 0,\ -3 - 1) = (4, 5, -4)$.
2. Vertical part: $(0, 5, 0)$ — the drone climbs 5 units.
3. Horizontal part: $(4, 0, -4)$ — over the ground it moves 4 units along
   $+x$ and 4 units along $-z$.
4. Return trip: $A - B = (-4, -5, 4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Mixing the order of the components. In $(4, 5, -4)$ the middle number is the
height only in a $y$-up world; in a $z$-up tool such as Blender the height is
the *last* component.
:::

## Case study: Comet Courier

*Comet Courier* is a mobile delivery game set in space. The courier ship
travels between depots on a 2D star map; each turn of the game lasts one
frame of movement. Depot Alpha is at $(1, 2)$, depot Beta at $(9, 6)$, and a
comet passes through $(5, 4)$. In the 3D version, stations float at
different heights. The exercises below and the Game challenge of the
interactive lesson use this map.

![The star map of *Comet Courier*: depots Alpha and Beta, the comet, and a ship flying with one velocity per frame.](images/comet-courier.png){#fig-courier width=88%}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 2 ("Vectors"), sections on the mathematical and geometric
definitions of a vector, specifying vectors with Cartesian coordinates, the
relationship between vectors and points, and negating a vector.

## Exercises

1. Classify as scalar or vector: (a) the fuel left in a car, 32 L; (b) a wind
   of 6 m/s from the north; (c) the gravity in a game; (d) the volume of the
   music.
2. Two enemies are at $(1, 1)$ and $(8, 3)$. Both move with velocity
   $(-1, 0)$ per frame. Are their velocity vectors equal? Explain.
3. An arrow starts at $(-2, 3)$ and ends at $(4, -1)$. Find its components.
4. An arrow with components $(3, -5)$ starts at $(2, 2)$. Where is its head?
5. Write the vector that points straight down with magnitude 4, and its
   negative.
6. Write $(-2, 5)$ and $(3, 0, -1)$ using the basis vectors $\mathbf{i}$,
    $\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{k}$.
7. A virtual joystick reports $(0, -1)$, then $(0, 0)$. Describe what the
    player is doing in each frame.
8. The player is at $P = (3, -2)$ and a health pack at $H = (-1, 5)$. Find the
   displacement from the player to the pack, and from the pack to the player.
9. Explain why the sum of two points, such as $(2, 3) + (5, 1)$, has no
   meaning in a game world, while their difference does.
10. A cannonball has velocity $(3, 2)$ per frame and starts at $(0, 1)$. Find its
   position after 1, 2 and 5 frames.
11. A platform moves from $(4, 1)$ to $(4, 9)$ in 4 frames at a constant
   velocity. Find the velocity per frame.
12. A ball at $(8, 2)$ moves with velocity $(-2, 1)$. After how many frames is
    its $x$-coordinate 0? Where is it then?
13. A game running at 60 fps moves an object 0.5 units per frame along $x$.
    How far does it move in one second? How far at 30 fps?
14. A hit from an enemy at $E = (5, 5)$ knocks the player at $P = (7, 4)$
    away from the enemy by one displacement $P - E$. Where does the player
    land?
15. A 3D camera moves from $(0, 10, -20)$ to $(4, 6, -12)$. Find the
    displacement, its vertical part and its horizontal part.
16. *Comet Courier*: find the displacement from Alpha to Beta and decide
    whether a ship that flies from Alpha with velocity $(2, 1)$ per frame
    passes through the comet's point. After how many frames?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. (a) scalar; (b) vector; (c) vector; (d) scalar.
2. Yes: same components $(-1, 0)$; position does not matter.
3. $(4 - (-2),\ -1 - 3) = (6, -4)$.
4. $(2 + 3,\ 2 - 5) = (5, -3)$.
5. $(0, -4)$; its negative is $(0, 4)$.
6. $-2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}$; $3\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}$.
7. Stick pushed fully down (walking down/backwards); then released — standing still (zero vector).
8. $H - P = (-4, 7)$; $P - H = (4, -7)$.
9. A point is a location; adding locations is undefined. The difference of two points is the displacement between them.
10. $(3, 3)$, $(6, 5)$, $(15, 11)$.
11. Total $(0, 8)$; $\mathbf{v} = (0, 2)$.
12. $8 - 2n = 0 \Rightarrow n = 4$; position $(0, 6)$.
13. 30 units per second; 15 units at 30 fps.
14. $P - E = (2, -1)$; $P' = (9, 3)$.
15. $(4, -4, 8)$; vertical $(0, -4, 0)$; horizontal $(4, 0, 8)$.
16. $(8, 4)$; yes: after 2 frames the ship is at $(5, 4)$.
:::
